newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish wheat price seen falling after import plan.
newsitem.headline: Turkish wheat price seen falling after import plan.

text.p: A plan by Turkey's state Grain Board (TMO) to import an unspecified amount of wheat will curb a surge in local prices caused by fears of restrictions on higher quality imported wheat, mistakenly subjected by the government to a zero-tolerance rule recently, millers and bakers said.

They also welcomed an official comment this morning that the government had cleared several cargoes of U.S. wheat it was holding up on grounds they might contain ergot fungus, and that it would issue a new regulation to ease the zero-tolerance rule.
"The TMO's imports will definitely ease wheat prices in the domestic market," Ilker Tanik, secretary-general of the Turkish Millers' Association, told Reuters.
"It can use both the wheat to be imported and its stocks to sell locally and this will boost flour exports," he said.

Millers' fears that high quality wheat may not be easily obtained after the fungus row led middle-men traders, estimated to hold about nine million tonnes in stocks, to raise prices to 27,000 lira per kg ($277 per tonne) from 20,000 two weeks ago.

"The TMO should step in and import wheat to stop the rise. This may even cause a drop in prices," said Yusuf Eksi, head of Ankara's Chamber of Bakers, shortly before the TMO said on Monday night it planned wheat imports "as soon as possible."
Officials said the TMO might invite tenders for small cargoes so as not to cause a rise in world prices. An analyst said the initial amount could be 100,000 to 150,000 tonnes of milling wheat.
Despite a rise in wheat output in 1996/97, millers prefer to import higher quality wheat to blend with the local crop.
Agriculture Minister Musa Demirci said Turkey imported 1.35 million tonnes of wheat by end-September and total imports might total two million tonnes by the end of the year.

He told Reuters on Tuesday the government decree amending the Farm Quarantine Act to introduce a 0.02-percent tolerance limit for ergot fungus in wheat imports instead of the present zero-tolerance would be published in the Official Gazette and take effect this week.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture decided last week to suspend wheat export certificates for sales to Turkey and warned it could extend the ban on exports of other grains to Turkey.

A government official said earlier in the day about 60,000 tonnes of U.S. dark northern spring wheat held at Tekirdag, Derince, Iskenderun and Izmir ports, were cleared of the fungus and would be allowed into the country.

"As of last night we allowed the U.S. wheat cargoes to come into Turkey," he said. "Instead of a zero-tolerance limit, we will from now seek a 0.02 percent limit for ergot disease in imported wheat," he told Reuters.

A zero-tolerance policy in the country's Farm Quarantine Act, designed for seed wheat only, was mistakenly applied to milling wheat and Demirci assured U.S. officials the mistake would be corrected in the new regulation.
Turkish farmers and millers as well as U.S. officials had said no country can guarantee zero-tolerance for ergot fungus.
Traders said some 100,000 tonnes of milling wheat, including cargoes waiting at ports, were heading for Turkey from the United States.

TMO officials said the government agency had about 1.2 million tonnes of wheat stocks including 500,000 tonnes of durum. They said TMO would sell part of its durum wheat to local pasta producers after an expected government decree which will enable it to sell locally at world prices, usually 20 percent cheaper than domestic prices, and the difference will be funded by the treasury.
